name: Christina
comment:
Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Christina McCarthy

name: Nancy
comment:
Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Nancy Carl
Carlton, OR 97111

Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Ms. Mary O'Brien

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Carol Healy
Burlington, CT 06013

I urge the Department to obey the law and follow common sense by withdrawing its plan to force

This opens up the possibility of sexual assault and other forms of harassment or abuse from people who do not share the same biological sex. 


This policy directly contradicts the very purpose of Title IX, which was passed in 1972 to promote equal opportunities for men and women in education, including athletics. Allowing biological males to compete with females goes against one of its primary goalsthat men and women should have equal access to sporting activities without discrimination based on sex. If enacted this policy sets a dangerous precedent that will undermine Title IXs original intent and put womens rights at risk. 


The Education Departments  proposed policy is dangerous and wrong on many levels. It undermines fairness by giving male-bodied athletes an advantage over their female-bodied counterparts, compromises safety by allowing male-bodied athletes access to female locker rooms, and violates Title IX by promoting discrimination based on gender identity rather than sex. This policy puts our daughters at risk.

name: Bill
comment:
Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule.
Thank you.

Sincerely,
Bill Stearns

This leaves the door open to dramatically confuse schools and states on what qualifies as legitimate reasons, such as physical harm, to keep women’s sports for biological women only.
 
I am calling on the Biden Administration to not put ideology and politics over girls and women. Please rescind this rule and make it clear for schools that women’s sports is for biological women only, as Title IX originally intended.
 
Thank you for considering this request.

I am writing to comment on the new proposed Title IX regulation in regard to “Sex-Related Eligibility Criteria for Male and Female Athletic Teams,”  published on April 13, 2023. 

While I appreciate that the Department acknowledges some of the many reasons single-sex sports are important, such as fairness and safety, I still have many concerns about the proposed test for determining when sex-based criteria may be permitted. 

Fairness and physical safety are, certainly, two extremely important factors when considering the impact of allowing boys and men to participate in female athletics. However, there are many other considerations that the current proposed regulation fails to take into account. The overall effect will worsen the participation of girls in sports, especially beginning in elementary and middle school, which will directly impact the number of girls who go on to participate in higher-level competitions or become lifelong athletes. These girls will be deprived of the  associated social, educational, and health benefits of participating in sports — all for the purpose of satisfying the desires of a small, but loud, minority. 

The proposed regulation would probably effectively ban single-sex sports in elementary and much of middle school. However, girls on average begin puberty between the ages of 8 - 13 (grades 3 - 7). Many girls are uncomfortable with their changing bodies around these ages, and would feel very self-conscious participating in sports with boys of the same age - not to mention sharing locker rooms with them. This aspect of the regulation is likely to limit young girls’ participation in sports, which will directly impact the number of girls who go on to participate in higher levels of competition.

The proposed regulation also claims that the existence of “no-cut” sports teams which are not highly selective and are “designed to encourage broad participation” are evidence that sex is irrelevant because sex is only important to safety and fairness. 

This, once again, ignores the very basic fact that many girls and women, especially in their difficult teenage years, simply will not feel comfortable participating in sports with their male peers. comment:
Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Mr. Mary Ann Medori

comment:
Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Maile Anthopoulos
Beaverton, OR 97008

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Daniela LANGLEY
Alva, FL 33920

Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Elizabeth Van De Kerkhove

name: Mary Ellen
comment:
Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female.

Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Mrs. Mary Ellen Ritsema

Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Vivian Jarvis

Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Roberta Apte
Marietta, GA 30066

name: Carman
comment:
Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Carman Coffman

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed Title IX policy changes related to the inclusion of transgender athletes in sports at all educational levels. While the intention to provide clarity and protections for transgender students is commendable, the proposed policy does not go far enough to ensure true inclusion for all athletes, regardless of gender identity.

Recently, a letter from a collective group of transgender legislators was submitted to the administration urging a revision of the proposed rules. The letter highlights the urgency of addressing the persistent discrimination and marginalization faced by transgender individuals in sports. It emphasizes the importance of creating policies that embrace and celebrate the achievements of transgender athletes without perpetuating unfounded and harmful stereotypes. As such, I support the legislators' call for revising the proposed policy with a presumption of full inclusion for transgender athletes and an obtainable pathway for participation at all levels of sports.

Furthermore, a recent study titled "Transgender Women Athletes and Elite Sport: A Scientific Review" emphasized the inconclusive findings of biomedical research on the competitive advantage of transgender athletes. The study also highlighted the importance of considering sociocultural factors in understanding athletic performance, rather than relying on testosterone levels or other physiological markers. This evidence suggests that the focus should be on addressing systemic inequalities in sports, rather than policing the bodies of transgender athletes.

The current proposed regulation lacks this presumption of inclusion and fails to mandate an attainable path for transgender students to participate in elite sports. To remedy these shortcomings, I propose the following changes:

Include a presumption of full inclusion for transgender athletes, allowing them to participate according to their gender identity.
Provide realistically attainable pathways for transgender students to participate in the sport that aligns with their gender identity at all levels of competition.

In conclusion, I strongly urge the Department to revise the proposed policy by incorporating the changes mentioned above in bullet points. By doing so, we can foster an inclusive, diverse, and equitable sports environment that respects and celebrates the rights and achievements of all athletes, including those who are transgender. Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

Sincerely,
Alexis Acebo

name: Clint
comment:
I am writing to elevate the American Psychological Association (APA) Services’ comments on this proposed rule. Specifically, I am urging the Department to please:

-	Move forward with its proposal to clarify school districts’ obligations to ensure safe, supportive, and non-discriminatory environments.
-	Move forward with its proposal to ensure that state laws categorically banning transgender, non-binary, and intersex students from participating in sports consistent with their gender identity are unlawful. 
-	Continue to rely on psychological science, research and data when developing education and civil rights policy. For example, please consider a 2020 policy statement adopted by APA and the National Association of School Psychologists recommending safer environments for gender diverse, transgender, and intersex students.
-	Clarify the exact criteria schools must use to determine which, if any, cases allow for the restriction of transgender, non-binary, and intersex student participation on sports teams consistent with their gender identity. This must include additional examples of the types of restrictions that would not meet the rule’s standards for exclusion.

This NPRM comes at a particularly troubling time for our nation’s LGBTQ+ students. Nationally representative CDC Youth Risk Behavioral Survey (YRBS) data show that lesbian, gay and bisexual youth are substantially more likely to have experienced all forms of violence and worse mental health outcomes than their heterosexual peers. In 2022 nearly 82% of LGBTQ+ students ages 13-21 reported feeling unsafe while at school last year, and 68% said they felt unsafe specifically because of their sexual orientation and gender identity or expression. In the same survey, LGBTQ+ students reported experiencing discriminatory policies or practices at school, with 11% reporting that school staff or coaches had prevented or discouraged them from playing sports because they identified as LGBTQ+.

As such, I am grateful for the opportunity to comment on this important and timely proposal.

name: Kimberly
comment:
Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Kimberly Clark

name: David

Please stop taking advantage of women and let them have their own sports.

I am writing to address concerns that my family and I have regarding the newly proposed rule, “Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Sex in Education Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance: Sex-Related Eligibility Criteria for Male and Female Athletic Teams” (RIN  1870-AA19; Docket ID ED-2022-OCR-0143; “Proposed Rule”). This Proposed Rule undercuts states that are protecting female athletes from ongoing discrimination and leaves women without protection when male students are allowed to join their teams. In fact, the majority of states have introduced legislation to protect female athletes, and so far twenty of them have passed those protections into law. This is not a minority viewpoint: it's common sense.

Women deserve a fair shot in sports, but when males are allowed to compete in female sports contests, that fair shot disappears. Males have an undeniable biological advantage over female athletes no matter the amount of testosterone suppression is taken–but the administration will allow males to compete with females anyway if this rule is finalized. When this happens, girls and women lose out on championships, scholarships, and other opportunities meant just for them.
 
The Proposed Rule states that if schools apply “a one-size-fits-all approach, they rely on overbroad generalizations that do not account for the nature of particular sports, the level of competition at issue, and the grade or education level of students to which they apply.” Those schools using that a standard across the board would thus not be in compliance with the rule as proposed. This leaves the door open to dramatically confuse schools and states on what qualifies as legitimate reasons, such as physical harm, to keep women’s sports for biological women only.
 
I am calling on the Biden Administration to not put ideology and politics over girls and women. Please rescind this rule and make it clear for schools that women’s sports is for biological women only, as Title IX originally intended.
 
Thank you for considering this request.

Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
Michael Gelfer

Allowing males, no matter how they self-identify, into women’s sports erases all pretense of fairness. This rule is blatantly sexist and unfair.

Do not implement this rule—it will hurt America’s daughters.

I am writing to comment on 34 CFR Part 106 [Docket ID ED–2022–OCR–0143] RIN 1870–AA19 Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Sex in Education Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance: Sex-Related Eligibility Criteria for Male and Female Athletic Teams, published on April 13, 2023. 

I am glad to see that the Department: (1) is no longer proposing to redefine sex to include “gender identity;” and (2) now appears to acknowledge the material reality of sex.

I oppose any efforts to redefine sex to include the nebulous category of “gender identity.” All federal efforts to redefine sex to include “gender identity,” including the Department’s July 2022 proposal, rely on the Biden Administration’s repeated mischaracterizations of the Supreme Court’s decision in the matter of Bostock v. Clayton County. 

I have several concerns with the Department’s most recent approach to amending the Title IX regulations. A federal district court has recently ruled that states (and the schools within them) may, consistent with both Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause of the Constitution, maintain single-sex sports. The Department cannot, as a matter of law, prohibit schools from doing something that the Constitution and federal law permit them to do. 

Schools can and should take into account differences in grade and education level, level of competition, and sports for purposes of determining which teams ought to be mixed sex. For example, it might be appropriate for schools to designate teams as mixed sex if there is a small number of girls who want to participate on a particular team but there are not enough such girls to create a female-only team. In such instances, and considering grade level and level of competition, mixed-sex teams might be appropriate. This should not, however, have anything to do with “gender identity.” 

The Department is now acknowledging the material reality of sex, which is good. But it should not assume that “gender identity” is a coherent concept that might, under some circumstances, be permitted to obscure the material reality of sex. The Department should also not expect schools to understand how to navigate all of this even if they want to maintain single-sex sports, which Title IX and the Constitution permit them to do.

Maintaining female-only sports is always substantially related to the achievement of an important educational objective (the inherent purpose of Title IX) and is the best way to "minimize harms to students".

This Proposed Rule undercuts states that are protecting female athletes from ongoing discrimination and leaves women without protection when male students are allowed to join their teams. In fact, the majority of states have introduced legislation to protect female athletes, and so far twenty of them have passed those protections into law. This is not a minority viewpoint: it's common sense.

Women deserve a fair shot in sports, but when males are allowed to compete in female sports contests, that fair shot disappears. Males have an undeniable biological advantage over female athletes no matter the amount of testosterone suppression is taken–but the administration will allow males to compete with females anyway if this rule is finalized. When this happens, girls and women lose out on championships, scholarships, and other opportunities meant just for them.
 
The Proposed Rule states that if schools apply “a one-size-fits-all approach, they rely on overbroad generalizations that do not account for the nature of particular sports, the level of competition at issue, and the grade or education level of students to which they apply.” Those schools using that a standard across the board would thus not be in compliance with the rule as proposed. This leaves the door open to dramatically confuse schools and states on what qualifies as legitimate reasons, such as physical harm, to keep women’s sports for biological women only.
 
I am calling on the Biden Administration to not put ideology and politics over girls and women. Please rescind this rule and make it clear for schools that women’s sports is for biological women only, as Title IX originally intended.
 
Thank you for considering this request.

Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students experience high rates of sex discrimination and harassment at school, which is linked to poor academic and health outcomes. Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Sincerely,
carl hujet
Green Bay, WI 54304

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed Title IX policy changes related to the inclusion of transgender athletes in sports at all educational levels. While the intention to provide clarity and protections for transgender students is commendable, the proposed policy does not go far enough to ensure true inclusion for all athletes, regardless of gender identity.

Recently, a letter from a collective group of transgender legislators was submitted to the administration urging a revision of the proposed rules. The letter highlights the urgency of addressing the persistent discrimination and marginalization faced by transgender individuals in sports. It emphasizes the importance of creating policies that embrace and celebrate the achievements of transgender athletes without perpetuating unfounded and harmful stereotypes. As such, I support the legislators' call for revising the proposed policy with a presumption of full inclusion for transgender athletes and an obtainable pathway for participation at all levels of sports.

Furthermore, a recent study titled "Transgender Women Athletes and Elite Sport: A Scientific Review" emphasized the inconclusive findings of biomedical research on the competitive advantage of transgender athletes. The study also highlighted the importance of considering sociocultural factors in understanding athletic performance, rather than relying on testosterone levels or other physiological markers. This evidence suggests that the focus should be on addressing systemic inequalities in sports, rather than policing the bodies of transgender athletes.

The current proposed regulation lacks this presumption of inclusion and fails to mandate an attainable path for transgender students to participate in elite sports. To remedy these shortcomings, I propose the following changes:

Include a presumption of full inclusion for transgender athletes, allowing them to participate according to their gender identity.
Provide realistically attainable pathways for transgender students to participate in the sport that aligns with their gender identity at all levels of competition.

In conclusion, I strongly urge the Department to revise the proposed policy by incorporating the changes mentioned above in bullet points. Dear Secretary Cardona,

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field.  Just recently, news broke of a female high school volleyball player who suffered long-term injuries last fall when she was spiked in the face by a male player on the opposing team. This young man was allowed to join the girl’s team because he identifies as a transgender female. 

Boys and girls, men and women currently have the chance to play on the teams aligned with their biological sex. Protecting women’s and girls’ sports doesn’t “ban” anyone from participating, it simply ensures that women’s sports can recognize biological reality rather than being bullied by individuals with a subjective (and often transitory) sense of “gender identity.” I oppose these changes to Title IX and object to the Biden Administration bullying schools and states by holding federal funds hostage to their transgender agenda.

I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule. 

Thank you.

Sincerely,
Beverlee Johannsen

name: Vicki
comment:
I am writing to comment on the new proposed Title IX regulation in regard to “Sex-Related Eligibility Criteria for Male and Female Athletic Teams,”  published on April 13, 2023. 

While I appreciate that the Department acknowledges some of the many reasons single-sex sports are important, such as fairness and safety, I still have many concerns about the proposed test for determining when sex-based criteria may be permitted. 

Fairness and physical safety are, certainly, two extremely important factors when considering the impact of allowing boys and men to participate in female athletics. However, there are many other considerations that the current proposed regulation fails to take into account. The overall effect will worsen the participation of girls in sports, especially beginning in elementary and middle school, which will directly impact the number of girls who go on to participate in higher-level competitions or become lifelong athletes. These girls will be deprived of the  associated social, educational, and health benefits of participating in sports — all for the purpose of satisfying the desires of a small, but loud, minority. 

The proposed regulation would probably effectively ban single-sex sports in elementary and much of middle school. However, girls on average begin puberty between the ages of 8 - 13 (grades 3 - 7). Many girls are uncomfortable with their changing bodies around these ages, and would feel very self-conscious participating in sports with boys of the same age - not to mention sharing locker rooms with them. This aspect of the regulation is likely to limit young girls’ participation in sports, which will directly impact the number of girls who go on to participate in higher levels of competition.

The proposed regulation also claims that the existence of “no-cut” sports teams which are not highly selective and are “designed to encourage broad participation” are evidence that sex is irrelevant because sex is only important to safety and fairness. 

This, once again, ignores the very basic fact that many girls and women, especially in their difficult teenage years, simply will not feel comfortable participating in sports with their male peers. This is because of more than just physical safety in high-contact sports. It is because boys will jeer, poke at girls, make comments about their bodies, and create a hostile environment where girls do not feel fully comfortable participating. Mixed-ex athletic leagues and teams, even at low levels of competition, are likely to exclude women and girls from these sports and deprive them of the associated benefits and opportunities.

The Department claims that male students who “transition at the onset of puberty … never gaining any potential advantages that the increased production of testosterone during male puberty may create.” This false oversimplification of the many differences between male and female bodies not only ignores other reasons why women and girls may not wish to participate in sports with male students, but also dangerously encourages child transition (including puberty blockers) as early as possible and supports the notion that children have a “gender identity.” I do not support any regulation that would codify “gender identity” (a regressive and vague concept that harms women and girls) into Title IX.

For these reasons, I urge the Department to return to the drawing board and consider regulations that explicitly protect the ability of schools to implement single-sex teams, leagues, and programs at any level of education and competition.

Thank you for your consideration.

Dear Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona,

I support the Department of Education (“Department”) taking action to protect the rights of transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to play school sports.  

I also urge the Department to strengthen its Title IX rule so that transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth can access the full benefits of an education, including by playing school sports as they are. Defending this right is crucial for these students’ well-being and ability to learn without discrimination.

Affirming policies that allow students to play sports consistent with their gender can reduce stigma, depression, and isolation, and contribute to positive academic outcomes like fewer absences, better grades, and higher chances of completing high school.   

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth need and deserve an opportunity to play school sports alongside their peers. This is especially the case in contexts that are primarily about the social, educational, and physical benefits of sport, rather than elite competition.  

Therefore, the Department should make clear that restrictions on transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students’ ability to play sports are never permitted at the K-12 or club college level. 

Transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students have been playing sports with their peers for years and with zero problems! In fact, barring trans women and girls from playing with other women and girls harms all women and girls because it can allow anyone to accuse any student athlete of not “really” being a woman or a girl.  Many times, this leads to “sex testing,” which includes horrific and invasive practices like genital inspections or hormonal tests for students to “prove” their gender. 
 
The Department should explicitly state that requiring sex testing of student athletes violates Title IX because such testing causes significant harm to affected students and is never necessary to advance an important educational objective. Sex testing invades students' privacy, is often enforced arbitrarily based on prejudice, and sends deeply stigmatizing and damaging messages to all youth that are completely inconsistent with a supportive educational environment. 
 
Discriminating against and demonizing some students because of who they are or how they look directly violates Title IX. I urge the Department to finalize and strengthen the Department’s Title IX rule to provide strong, clear protections for transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students to participate fully in sports consistent with their gender identity.

Kristin Walters

I write to oppose the proposed Title IX rule that would completely reverse the current protections for women and girls in sports. 

This rule’s interpretation of Title IX would prohibit schools from establishing policies for sports based on biological sex. Instead, it would create uncomfortable, even dangerous, situations for student athletes, and would put teachers, staff, and coaches who care about students and the reality of biological sex in the untenable position of violating their beliefs.

The proposal, if adopted, would protect only a claimed “transgender” status, which will allow boys and men to compete on teams once reserved for girls and women. This is a blatant attempt to undermine 50 years of Title IX protections for female athletes, as well as the many states and localities that have passed legislation to protect women’s and girls’ sports. The federal government should not pressure local schools and school districts to ignore biology, safety, and fairness. 

The proposed rule would unreasonably prohibit boys-only and girls-only sports teams in elementary schools. I do not believe that the Department of Education is acting in good faith when it claims it will consider the needs of middle, high school, or college aged women and girls by requiring them to make their case and convince you to allow them to retain their sex-based rights under a reimagined Title IX. Women should not have to petition the government to in order to keep their basic rights to safety and fairness. 

The abolition of male and female categories will allow males to access private spaces previously reserved for women and girls. Coaches will be forced to supervise opposite sex young athletes in locker rooms, while girls and women will be forced to share showers, changing areas, and possibly beds or bedrooms (when traveling for games) with boys and men based on “gender identity” claims. Physical differences between boys and girls will put girls at higher risk of injury on the playing field. I ask that you protect the integrity of women’s athletics and Title IX by withdrawing this proposed rule.

Sincerely,
Ann Metzler
